sections.body:
The smartphone era organized the world's services into apps, and apps into screens of controls. Every want had a procedure: open the app, find the feature, fill the form, confirm. Humans learned the procedures; the software waited for them.

AI agents invert the arrangement. The user states an intention — 'find me a train that gets me home by seven and is under twenty dollars' — and the agent performs the procedure across several apps, reading screens, filling forms, confirming details. The user's relationship with the software stops being manual.

This is not a small interaction change; it is a change in who operates whom. For the first time since computing began, the default user of software may become another piece of software. The screen, designed for human fingers, becomes a side channel that agents read and humans occasionally check.
examples: She said 'reschedule my dentist appointment to next month'; the agent opened the booking app, found the calendar, and returned with three options.
sections.heading: From buttons to intentions

sections.body:
The app economy was built on attention capture: each company fenced its service inside its own interface, because the interface was where the advertising, the data and the loyalty lived. Agents ignore fences. They traverse services on the user's behalf, which turns every walled garden into a corridor.

This breaks several business patterns at once. Interfaces designed to be addictive become irrelevant when nobody looks at them. Notifications lose power when an agent screens them. Lock-in weakens when switching costs are paid by software, not by a human relearning a new app.

The response is already visible: services exposing machine interfaces — APIs and structured access — for agents, while human-facing design quietly declines in importance. In the long run, the companies that win may be the ones whose services are easiest for agents to use faithfully, not the ones whose interfaces are most engaging to human eyes. Software competes to be chosen by machines.
examples: The food delivery app noticed half its orders now arrived through assistants, and redesigned around clean machine access instead of flashy banners.
sections.heading: Why every company built a wall, and what breaks

sections.body:
Delegation has a boundary, and with software it runs through preference and responsibility. Agents can compare options, but choosing between them often involves values no model holds: Is the cheapest flight worth a four-hour layover with a tired child? Is the convenient doctor the one I trust? Preferences like these are formed by living, not by optimizing.

Responsibility sets a harder boundary. When an agent books the wrong flight, sends the wrong message or buys the wrong stock, the consequences belong to the human who delegated. Keeping meaningful control means keeping meaningful visibility: knowing what the agent did, being able to interrupt, and reserving final approval for what matters.

The healthiest model emerging is a division of labor: agents handle procedure, humans handle preference and responsibility. The app era made people operate machines; the agent era makes machines operate software — with people doing the distinctly human parts that remain.
examples: The agent handles the three booking apps; he handles the single question that decides: does this trip work for the family?
sections.heading: What the human keeps

sections.body: These terms describe the shift from human-operated to agent-operated software.
sections.heading: The vocabulary of software that serves

terms.example: The agentic app did not wait to be told; it noticed the delayed flight and rebooked the connection.
terms.gloss: Software designed to act toward goals with a degree of autonomy rather than waiting for each command.

terms.example: The adaptive interface showed the departure board first on travel day, and the meeting notes every Monday.
terms.gloss: A user interface that changes according to context, intent and history rather than showing fixed menus.

terms.example: Her intent was 'a quiet table for two on Friday'; the commands involved three apps and a phone call.
terms.gloss: A statement of what the user wants to achieve, as opposed to the commands that achieve it.

terms.example: Task automation moved the invoice from email to accounting to payment confirmation while she drank coffee.
terms.gloss: The performance of multi-step procedures by software without human operation of each step.

terms.example: The assistant used the bank's API to check the balance — no screen, no password typing.
terms.gloss: Application programming interface: a structured way for software to use another service, made for machines rather than humans.

terms.example: In ambient computing, the house adjusts the heating and the agent adjusts the schedule, and nobody opened an app.
terms.gloss: Computing woven into the environment so that it acts in the background without demanding attention.

sections.body: For decades, software showed its work on screen because humans were the operators. As agents take over operation, the interface shrinks to a summary of what was done — a receipt to check, not a machine to run. Designing for trust then matters more than designing for engagement.
sections.heading: The screen is becoming a receipt

sections.body:
The skills the app era demanded — memorizing procedures, navigating menus, managing many logins — are depreciating. The skills the agent era rewards are different: stating goals clearly, dividing labor between self and software wisely, auditing results, and knowing when to take the controls back.

There is also a cultural adjustment. Software that acts can feel like loss of control or like relief, depending on how it is built and governed. The demand that will shape the next decade is simple to state and hard to deliver: agents that are powerful under the hood and honest at the surface, showing what they did in language a tired human can check at a glance.

The relationship between people and software is becoming what it perhaps always should have been: people bring intentions and judgment, software brings memory and speed, and the division of labor is negotiated openly. The app taught us to serve the interface. The agent promises the opposite — and keeping that promise will be the work of years.
examples: He checks the agent's summary each evening for two minutes — not to operate the day, but to own it.
sections.heading: Learning to live with software that acts

item.summary: For fifteen years, software meant screens: tap here, scroll there, learn each app's menus. This article examines the shift now underway: AI agents that operate apps on our behalf, interfaces that adapt to intent, and the end of the era in which every task required a human pressing buttons.
item.title: The Future of Mobile Apps: When AI Uses Software for Us
